title: About
text:
I’m Alejandro Hinojosa, a senior in the Department of Psychology and Neuroscience at Baylor University. I’m interested in how people learn from what happens to them, and in how mathematical models of that learning can help explain differences in decision-making, including in psychiatric conditions.
My research so far is an independent project: implementing reinforcement-learning models of the Iowa Gambling Task, testing extensions with predictions written in advance, and running the analyses on Baylor’s Kodiak computing cluster. I also work in a research lab at Baylor.
Outside research, I read a lot of philosophy and literature, and I write about both.

title: Research
text:
preprint in preparation · code and full write-up on GitHub

The Iowa Gambling Task asks people to draw cards from four decks. Two decks pay well at first but lose money over time, and two pay less but come out ahead. The task is widely used to study decision-making, including in addiction and other clinical conditions. Computational models split each person’s choices into the processes behind them: how quickly they learn from wins and from losses, how strongly they stick with a deck, and how much they explore.
I implemented three standard models and fit them to 162 healthy adults, then tested a series of extensions, writing my predictions down before each analysis. The one that held up best restores outcome curvature to the ORL model: the felt size of a win or a loss grows more slowly than its dollar amount. ORL + α predicted held-out choices best of eight models, and on a second sample of 70 people, all five predictions written in advance were met.


first sample · N = 16281% below 1 · median 0.30



held-out sample · N = 7089% below 1 · median 0.32


00.5α = 11.52
Each dot is one person's α in ORL + α. At α = 1 (lavender line), a win or loss counts in proportion to its size; below 1, large outcomes count for less than their size. About a quarter to a third of people sit at the lower limit, where only whether an outcome was a gain or a loss matters.

No single model described everyone well, though. Different people were predicted best by different models, which led to the next project.

title: Research
text:
Mixing and switching between models

in progress · preregistered on OSF

If people differ in which model fits them, each person might be a blend of strategies, or might switch strategies partway through the task. In exploratory analyses, a weighted mix of eight models predicted choices better than any one model, and a model that lets strategies switch over the session did better still. I’m now testing whether this holds in 440 new participants, and whether data simulated with no switching at all would produce the same result.

title: Research
text:
Next

Tiny recurrent neural networks, as a benchmark for how much predictable structure the models miss.
An EEG study of whose prediction errors the brain tracks after feedback: one model’s, or a blend.
